title: See our trouble
hookLine: look upon our affliction and redeem us
last: EASIER WHEN YOU DON'T LET IT BUILD UP.

cards: There's a particular kind of loneliness in trouble nobody notices. The rent that's late again. The marriage that looks fine from the outside.

The test results you haven't told anyone about. Often, before we want anyone to fix it, we want someone to see it. A friend who says, that sounds really hard, can matter more than one who rushes to solutions.
The seventh blessing of the Amidah opens with exactly that request. Before rescue, before redemption: look.

teach.b: The seventh blessing says: look upon our affliction, and fight our fight, and redeem us quickly, for Your name's sake, for You are a mighty redeemer. Blessed are You, Redeemer of Israel.
In Hebrew it opens re'eh ve'onyenu: see our affliction. That word for affliction, oni, goes back to the burning bush.

teach.h: I HAVE SURELY SEEN, AT THE BUSH.
teach.b: There God says to Moses, in the old Jewish translation: "I have surely seen the affliction of My people." Same word. The Exodus starts with God seeing, so the blessing asks God to do again what began the first redemption.
Fight our fight is a phrase from the Psalms: take up our case, be on our side in the quarrel. You may remember go'el, the redeemer who buys back.
Before the Amidah, the Shema's blessing ended ga'al Yisrael, who redeemed, in the past. Here it's go'el Yisrael, who redeems, now.
The Talmud, in Megillah 17b, says this blessing is seventh because redemption is expected in a seventh year.

teach.h: FOR THE TROUBLES THAT KEEP COMING.
teach.b: The commentator Rashi adds that it isn't about the great final redemption, which comes later in the Amidah, but the daily troubles that keep coming.
On public fast days, the leader adds a short prayer right after it, aneinu: answer us.
The blessing doesn't ask for trouble to vanish. It asks, first, that it be seen, and then that someone take our side.

how: Re'eh ve'onyenu is the seventh blessing of the weekday Amidah, ending go'el Yisrael; on public fast days the leader adds the prayer Aneinu between this blessing and the next.

games.q: a friend tells you about a hard week. the Amidah's seventh blessing asks God to do something first. what?
games.why: re'eh ve'onyenu: see our affliction. the Exodus began when God saw; rescue follows seeing.

practice: Find one trouble you're carrying right now, the one you usually describe as fine, and name it plainly in a short sentence, without softening it and without making it bigger.
If you pray, you can say it as a request to be seen: look at this. If you don't, let yourself be the one who sees it, and stay with it for a few breaths instead of looking away.

wordCard.voice: Oni. Affliction — the word from the burning bush, where God saw it, now asked again in the Amidah: see our affliction, and fight our fight.
